History:
- Presenting complaint: 3-day history of watery then very loose diarrhoea with vomiting and subjective high temperature.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began 3 days ago; diarrhoea started watery then became very loose; continues and not improving. Vomiting began this morning after breakfast (~2 hours prior to consult) and patient is unable to keep fluids down.
- Stool/urine: At least four bowel movements today; no blood in stool or urine. Passed urine ~1 hour before consult.
- Pain: Intermittent central abdominal pain localized around the navel, tender to touch, associated with urgent need to defecate when pain occurs.
- Exposures/contacts: Household contact (brother) with similar symptoms; patient reports others at brother’s school have same illness. No recent travel.
- Associated symptoms/negatives: Subjective fever ("literally boiling"); denies rash. No prior chronic bowel problems; normal baseline bowel habit — daily once in morning. No recent surgeries or known abdominal disease.
- Social/functional: Lives with brother and mother. Works as a graphic designer; working from home today due to symptoms.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: None reported.
- Surgical history: None reported.
- Allergies: Not documented (patient did not report allergies).
- Medications:
  - Vitamin D daily — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Occasional ibuprofen for menstrual cramps — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Oral rehydration salts (ORS; salt-sugar mix) taken ~3 times daily for past 2 days.
- Tobacco/drugs/alcohol: Does not smoke. Drinks alcohol occasionally ("a pint from time to time"). No recreational drug use reported.
- Gynecologic: Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago. Not on contraception. Not sexually active currently.

Physical Examination:
- No clinician-recorded vital signs or exam findings in transcript.
- Patient-reported/observed findings:
  - Central (periumbilical) abdominal tenderness.
  - Alert and able to converse.
  - Passed urine ~1 hour prior (suggests some ongoing urine output).
  - No throat swelling reported; no rash.
- Relevant negatives: No blood in stool or urine; no chronic bowel disease history.

Impression:
- Likely infectious gastroenteritis (probable viral etiology given household contact/outbreak), with concern for dehydration due to persistent vomiting and inability to retain oral fluids; bacterial infection not excluded — stool testing recommended.

Management Plan:
- Immediate recommendations given:
  - Continue oral rehydration salts (ORS) in very small, frequent sips to minimize vomiting.
  - Consume bland, light foods if tolerated (e.g., toast or biscuit); avoid fruit, vegetables, milk, and other foods that may worsen symptoms.
  - Urgent clinic appointment to assess hydration status and to collect stool sample for microbiological testing.
  - If symptoms worsen or patient becomes more unwell, go to Accident & Emergency (A&E) for urgent assessment.
- Arrangements:
  - Clinician to arrange an urgent appointment through support line for in-clinic hydration assessment and stool sample submission.
  - Patient advised to call back / present to A&E if deteriorates before appointment.
- No prescriptions or investigations ordered during the call beyond plan for stool testing and hydration check.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with 3 days of watery/very loose diarrhoea, vomiting, subjective fever, and central abdominal pain with household contact who is similarly unwell. Most likely viral gastroenteritis but bacterial causes need exclusion. Plan is urgent clinic assessment for hydration status and stool sample testing; continue small frequent sips of ORS and simple diet; attend A&E if worse.

Key Takeaways:
- Keep taking ORS in very small, frequent sips even if vomiting; passing urine is a positive sign of some hydration.
- Eat bland/light foods if tolerated; avoid fruit, vegetables, and milk.
- Attend urgent clinic appointment for hydration check and stool testing; go to A&E if condition worsens.

Next Steps:
- Urgent in-person clinic appointment to check hydration and obtain stool sample (to be booked via support line by the service).
- If unable to attend clinic promptly or if patient deteriorates (increasing vomiting, decreased urine output, worsening vital signs), present to A&E for urgent care and possible IV rehydration.
- Laboratory testing: stool microbiology (sample to be sent to lab) — specifics to be arranged at clinic visit.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate) are not documented.
  - Physical examination by clinician is not documented.
  - Allergy status not explicitly recorded.
  - Exact plan for stool sample collection and transport details not documented.
  - No documentation of whether antiemetic or antimicrobial therapy was considered/prescribed.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - None identified.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Transcript is generally clear and audible though there are brief pauses/interruptions and a few inaudible short segments; essential clinical information is present.
